sectionsContent.title: Unit 5 Test · Multiple Choice + Polarity Sort

concept.summary: Copy these into Edulastic. Questions 1–17 are multiple choice. The sort uses the eight structure pictures, saved as separate image files (sort_*.png) in the same Drive folder. Suggested sort stem: "Sort each molecule as polar or nonpolar. EN: H 2.20 · Be 1.57 · C 2.55 · N 3.04 · O 3.44 · F 3.98 · Si 1.90 · Cl 3.16."

items.stem: How many valence electrons go into the Lewis structure of SCl₂?
items.why: A counts each Cl as 1. B forgets the S. D gives every atom 8. S 6 + Cl 7 × 2 = 20.

items.stem: After you COUNT, build the SKELETON and FILL, the central atom has only 6 electrons. What does the CHECK step tell you to do?
options: Turn an outer lone pair into a double bond
Add 2 more electrons to the central atom
Swap the central atom with an outer atom
Leave it; every atom is stable with 6
items.why: B changes the electron total. C treats it as a skeleton error. D stretches the boron exception to every atom.

items.stem: Which atom goes in the center of the Lewis structure for HCN?
options: H, because it is written first
None; a linear molecule has no center
items.why: A: H is never the center atom. C: the least EN atom goes in the center (C 2.55 < N 3.04). D confuses shape with skeleton.

items.stem: According to VSEPR theory, electron pairs around a central atom...
options: spread as far apart as they can
crowd onto one side of the atom
attract each other to form bonds
always sit at 90° in one flat plane
items.why: Slide 13. B and C think the pairs attract. D is the flat-molecule picture.

items.stem: Molecule X has 4 bonding pairs on its central atom and 109.5° bond angles. Molecule Y has 3 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair, and its angles are less than 109.5°. Why?
options: Y's lone pair repels more strongly and squeezes the bonds closer
Y has fewer bonds, so its bonds are shorter
The outer atoms in Y attract each other
Y's central atom is always more electronegative
items.why: Slide 13 must-write: lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs. B confuses length with angle. C puts IMF thinking inside a molecule. D has nothing to do with the angle.

items.stem: How many electron groups are on the central C in HCN?
items.why: C counts each pair of the triple bond; a triple bond is ONE group (slide 17). B adds a lone pair C does not have. D also counts N's lone pair.

items.stem: PCl₅ has 5 bonding pairs and 0 lone pairs on P. What is its shape?
items.why: A assumes P cannot pass 8. C is the 5 bonds + 1 lone pair shape. D miscounts 6 groups.

items.stem: SO₂ has 2 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair on S. Which pair gives its electron geometry / molecular geometry?
items.why: B swaps the two names. C ignores the lone pair (the CO₂ habit). D counts 4 groups.

items.stem: BCl₃ has three polar B–Cl bonds (ΔEN 1.12), but the molecule is nonpolar. Why?
options: The three equal dipoles are spread symmetrically and cancel
Bonds between nonmetals are always nonpolar
B has only 6 electrons, so no dipole forms
The lone pairs on Cl cancel the dipoles
items.why: B equates bond type with polarity. C mixes up the octet exception with polarity. D thinks outer lone pairs decide polarity.
SCl₂ is bent (2 lone pairs on S), so its polar S–Cl bonds do not cancel. SF₆ and XeF₄ are symmetric, so their polar bonds cancel. Br₂: same atoms, ΔEN 0.

items.stem: For the H–Cl bond, which way does the dipole arrow point?
options: Toward H, because it has fewer electrons
Both ways; HCl has no direction
items.why: Slide 10: the arrow points toward δ−, cross at δ+. B and C reverse it. D ignores the partial charges.

items.stem: An N–H bond has a ΔEN of 0.84. What type of bond is it?
items.why: 0.40 to 1.80 is polar covalent. A needs under 0.40, C over 1.80. D is a metal–metal bond.
P–H: 2.20 − 2.19 = 0.01, under 0.40. O–H 1.24, C–O 0.89 and N–F 0.94 are polar covalent.

items.stem: In a polar covalent bond, the atom with the higher electronegativity becomes...
items.why: Slide 9: the shared electrons shift toward the higher-EN atom. B reverses it. C is an ionic bond. D is a nonpolar bond.

items.stem: After the single bonds are drawn, where do the remaining electrons go first?
options: On the outer atoms, as lone pairs
items.why: Slide 14: FILL puts lone pairs on the outer atoms first; leftovers go on the center. C skips the CHECK step. D breaks the electron count.

items.stem: A central atom has 4 electron groups: 2 bonding pairs and 2 lone pairs. What is the molecular shape?
items.why: B ignores the lone pairs. C names the electron geometry, not the shape. D is 3 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair.

items.stem: Two molecules both have 4 electron groups on the central atom. One is tetrahedral and the other is bent. What is different?
options: The bent one has 2 lone pairs on the central atom
The bent one has a double bond
The tetrahedral one has lone pairs on the central atom
items.why: Same electron groups, but lone pairs are not counted in the shape name: 4 bonding pairs = tetrahedral, 2 bonding + 2 lone = bent. B: a double bond is still one group. C: bond type, not shape. D reverses it.

keyNotes: No multiple-choice or sort molecule is on the written test or the study guide.

Sort reasoning: H₂O, NH₃ have lone pairs on the center (asymmetric); CH₃Cl has one different atom; HF has one polar bond. CH₄ and SiH₄ have nonpolar bonds (0.35, 0.30); N₂ has ΔEN 0; BeCl₂ is linear, so its two polar bonds (1.59) cancel.
